Abstract
One of the most crucial steps for preparing datasets for machine learning is Feature Selection (FS). It aims to identify the 
smallest subset of features that best capture the essence of all features in a given dataset. However, it is time-consuming 
to solve the FS problem using exact methods due to the exponential complexity of the FS problem in high-dimensional 
datasets (HDDs). Therefore, approximation methods, such as meta-heuristic algorithms, can be used to solve the FS prob­
lem in a reasonable time. The Artificial Rabbit Optimization (ARO) algorithm is a new optimization search method that 
models the social activities of rabbits in the wild to solve complex continuous optimization problems. In its basic form, 
ARO cannot be applied directly to solve binary optimization problems, such as the FS problem in HDDs. Besides, ARO 
suffers from some performance shortcomings such as premature convergence and limited exploration ability. Therefore, 
this research study introduces the Binary Improved ARO Algorithm (BIARO) to provide more efficient solutions for the 
FS problem in HDDs. BIARO improves the search process of the ARO algorithm in four ways. First, it implements the 
Gaussian perturbation (GP) method at the beginning of the ARO algorithm to add stochastic dynamic behavior to the 
creation process of the initial binary combinations of features. Second, it utilizes the Adaptive β-hill climbing (ABHC) 
method in the evolution process of ARO to improve its global search and exploration abilities. Third, it uses the Mixed 
Opposition-based Learning (MOBL) approach in the evolution process of ARO to explore the opposite solutions of the 
best and worst rabbits in the population of rabbits. Finally, it employs binary conversion methods to compute binary 
subsets of features from the real numbers produced by the evolution processes of the ARO and ABHC algorithms. The 
performance of BIARO, six machine learning classifiers, and nine efficient, popular, nature-inspired FS algorithms was 
investigated using 21 real-life HDDs from different fields. According to experimental results, BIARO achieved excep­
tional results in real-life HDDs, with average accuracy values between 0.69 and 1, average precision values in the range 
of 0.67 to 1, average F1 scores in the range of 0.67 to 1, average Recall values in the range of 0.67 to 1, and a perfor­
mance improvement rate between − 2 and 66. Furthermore, statistical verification methods were employed to evaluate the 
dependability of the experimental results. The statistical results show that BIARO scored the highest rank based on the 
fitness values for 14 HDDs, with a p-value of 0.001. Besides, it shows that it scored the highest rank based on the number 
of selected features for 18 HDDs, with a p-value of 0.001. All experimental and statistical results provide evidence that 
BIARO is an efficient FS method for HDDs.

1  Introduction
In the current digital era, the creation and gathering of 
massive volumes of information have become essential 
to almost every part of our life [1, 2]. From e-commerce 
and social media to healthcare and scientific research, vast 
amounts of data are being created at an unprecedented 
rate [3]. This boom in data output has given birth to new 
opportunities and difficulties alike. The immensity of this 
data flood is both a blessing and a hardship. On one side, it 
delivers a wealth of important information that may drive 
decision-making, stimulate innovation, and alter industries. 
On the other side, a large number of these datasets represent 
enormous barriers in terms of storage, processing, and, most 
crucially, extracting meaningful knowledge before trying 
to use it by different algorithms, such as Machine Learn­
ing (ML) algorithms [4]. Preprocessing high-dimensional 
datasets (HDDs) is critical to assure data quality, remove 
noise, and prepare the data for successful analysis and mod­
eling [5–7]. This necessary step is used depending on the 
nature of the dataset used and the analysis tasks, such as 
Data Cleaning and Transformation, Feature Selection (FS) 
and Feature Extraction.
1.1  Motivations
As we mentioned previously, one of the most important 
steps in preparing data for use by algorithms is FS, which 
selects the most relevant information in the data and boosts 
the performance and interpretability of the models. Four 
groups of FS algorithms can be distinguished depending 
on the methods of assessment: embedding, filter, hybrid-
based, and wrapper approaches [8]. FS is a vital phase in 
ML and data analysis, but it is not without its obstacles and 
issues. It is sought to be solved using several approaches, 
the most notable of which is optimization methods because 
they help to improve efficiency, Cost Reduction, Enhanced 
Decision-Making, and Quality Improvement. Binary opti­
mization methods are used to identify the best combination 
of binary choice variables in a task. Binary Particle Swarm 
Optimization (BPSO), Binary Genetic Algorithm (BGA), 
Ant Colony Optimization for Binary Problems (ACO-B) [4, 
9], Cuckoo Search (CS), Simulated Annealing, and Whale 
Optimization Algorithm (WOA) are examples of optimiza­
tion algorithms that are used in FS. The best solutions are 
produced under conditions that lead to the best results, such 
as the shortest possible time, the lowest computational cost, 
and the fewest number of features [10–15]. However, these 
FS approaches have several limitations such as premature 
convergence and trapping in local optima (e.g., BPSO and 
BGA stagnating in high-dimensional spaces), high compu­
tational costs (e.g., pheromone updates with ACO-B are 
extremely expensive, while Simulated Annealing converges 
slowly), parameter setting sensitivity (e.g., BPSO is sensi­
tive to inertia weight and BGA is sensitive to crossover and 
mutation rates), and with some algorithms, the challenge 
of binary adaption (e.g., losing information in converting 
from continuous to binary), as well as a lack of awareness 
regarding feature interactions. These techniques also have 
scalability issues in high-dimensional data, and due to the 
random nature of most of such algorithms, yield inconsis­
tent results. This strongly emphasizes the need for hybrid 
or adaptive approaches, with an aim of strengthening the 
effective methods.
The Artificial Rabbit Optimization method, which is 
abbreviated as ARO, is a modern swarm intelligence algo­
rithm that models the social activities of rabbits [16, 17]. 
ARO tries to discover the optimum solution to a given 
problem by iteratively exploring the solution space. The FS 
problem in HDDs is one example of a binary optimization 
problem that cannot be directly solved using the basic ARO 
algorithm. This is because ARO was originally developed to 
solve continuous optimization problems. Additionally, ARO 
has certain performance issues, such as early convergence 
and restricted exploration capabilities [1, 17]. In fact, these 
problems are considered inherited problems in the optimiza­
tion field [18–21]. Many algorithms, such as Particle Swarm 
Optimization (PSO), Genetic Algorithm (GA), and Differ­
ential Evolution, suffer from several performance restric­
tions. First, these algorithms require high computational 
cost because of their mutation and crossover operators. Sec­
ond, they suffer from the premature convergence problem 
when implemented in high-dimensional problems. Third, 
the binary mutation in these algorithms might not provide 
a significant increase in performance in binary problems. 
Fourth, these algorithms cannot maintain high population 
diversity all through their optimization process. Finally, the 
binary versions of these algorithms, such as BPSO, BGA, 
and Binary DE, may sometimes produce low-quality feature 
subsets for the FS problem in HDDs [10–14].
1.2  Contributions
The FS problem is commonly regarded as a multimodal 
optimization problem. This is because the binary search 
space of FS may contain several local optima that exhibit 
similar performance. For example, two different combina­
tions of features in the FS space may have similar accuracy.

Another important issue is that the relationships between

This work’s primary objective is to improve the origi­
nal ARO algorithm to solve the FS problem in HDDs. This 
is accomplished by introducing the Binary Improved ARO 
Algorithm (BIARO). BIARO includes four modifications to 
the ARO algorithm:
	
●
Enhancing the initialization stage of ARO using the 
Gaussian perturbation method [23] to improve its popu­
lation diversity.
	
●
Improving the iterative search process of ARO using the 
adaptive β-hill climbing (ABHC) algorithm [24] and the 
Mixed Opposition-based Learning (MOBL) approach 
[23]. These improvements in the exploration process of 
ARO help in overcoming the premature convergence 
problem.
	
●
Using Binary Transfer Functions (BTFs) to generate bi­
nary FS combinations for the FS problem from the con­
tinuous real-number combinations produced by ARO.

2  Literature review
This section is divided into two parts: popular nature-
inspired FS methods are reviewed in the first part, while 
in the second part, some popular hybrid nature-inspired FS 
methods are discussed.
2.1  Metaheuristic FS methods
As was already indicated, FS has been handled as a data 
mining process using a range of approaches, such as filter-
based approaches [25], wrapper-based approaches [26], 
embedded approaches [27], and hybrid approaches [28]. 
The focus of this work is on using the wrapper-based for 
FS process. In wrapper-based methods, a machine learning 
classifier is frequently coupled with a greedy search method 
to select the best descriptive subset of features from a large 
set of features for a particular dataset. The most successful 
and greediest search algorithms are meta-heuristic ones.
Awadallah et al. [29] suggested using the Horse herd 
Optimization Algorithm (HOA) in binary form to solve 
and address the FS problem. HOA mimics the behavior of 
horses to survive in nature. The authors combined improve­
ments to Binary HOA (BHOA). First, it uses three forms 
of BTFs for the binarization of HOA, which are the S-, V-, 
and U-shaped BTFs. Second, it employs three crossover 
operators, which are uniform, two-point, and one-point, to 
improve the effectiveness of HOA for FS. The results of 
BHOA were evaluated according to several metrics such as 
computational time, accuracy, number of features selected, 
quality, and fitness values. After the evaluation, it was found 
that the best version is the one that integrates the S-shaped 
BTF with the one-point crossover method. The authors 
evaluated the study against 21 modern methods. In conclu­
sion, BHOA has proven to be accurate and effective com­
pared to other algorithms.
As for the Salp Swarm Algorithm (SSA), an improve­
ment to it has been proposed by Faris et al. [30]. The pro­
posed model was called Binary SSA (BSSA), and it was 
modelled using two approaches. First, it uses eight S- and 
V-shaped BTFs to enable SSA to deal with binary values in 
FS. Second, it investigates enhancing the exploration ability 
of SSA by integrating eight BTFS with a binary crossover 
operator. The researchers used 22 UCI datasets to compare 
the proposed versions of BSSA with other approaches and 
concluded that BSSA3 (SSA, S-shaped, binary crossover) 
was the best among the other versions in terms of accuracy.

The β-hill climbing algorithm was recently introduced

provide accurate and high-performance solutions to vari­

transfer function to convert from a discrete representa­

model, 22 datasets were used, and the proposed algorithm 
was compared with three research methods, Local and ten 
metaheuristics methods. According to the findings, the β
-hill climbing algorithm is a better FS method than the other 
tested algorithms.

3.4  Artificial rabbit optimization algorithm
3.4.1  Inspiration
The Artificial Rabbit Algorithm (ARO) is one of the rela­
tively modern algorithms inspired by the behavior of rabbits 
in nature in the process of searching for foods innovated in

strategies and algorithms that assess the value and contribu­

accuracy, efficiency, dimensionality reduction, experimen­
tation, and interpretability. FS methods can be grouped into 
three main categories [60]:

Consistency-Based Filters, Statistical Filters, and Rank­
ing Filters, characterized by their simplicity and quick­
ness. They evaluate the importance of specific features 
independently of each other and the machine learning 
model to be used [61].
2.	 Wrapper: It is divided into Subset Search, Recursive

Backward Elimination, and Genetic Algorithms. In this

subsets of features are discovered through iterative test­
ing and training models. The difference between them 
is that forward selection starts with an empty feature set 
and then starts adding features gradually, while back­
ward selection starts with the entire set and then starts 
deleting them one by one. As for genetic algorithms, 
Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) is one of the most 
advanced wrapper techniques, but it is one of the most 
expensive techniques [62].

niques, Decision Tree-Based Methods, and Feature

without much administration costs. Hence, policymakers 
should thus consider promoting standardized benchmarking 
of such advanced FS methods to ensure transparency, repro­

industries.

Abstract: One of the most crucial steps for preparing datasets for machine learning is Feature Selection (FS). It aims to identify the smallest subset of features that best capture the essence of all features in a given dataset. However, it is time-consuming to solve the FS problem using exact methods due to the exponential complexity of the FS problem in high-dimensional datasets (HDDs). Therefore, approximation methods, such as meta-heuristic algorithms, can be used to solve the FS prob­ lem in a reasonable time. The Artificial Rabbit Optimization (ARO) algorithm is a new optimization search method that models the social activities of rabbits in the wild to solve complex continuous optimization problems. In its basic form, ARO cannot be applied directly to solve binary optimization problems, such as the FS problem in HDDs. Besides, ARO suffers from some performance shortcomings such as premature convergence and limited exploration ability. Therefore, this research study introduces the Binary Improved ARO Algorithm (BIARO) to provide more efficient solutions for the FS problem in HDDs. BIARO improves the search process of the ARO algorithm in four ways. First, it implements the Gaussian perturbation (GP) method at the beginning of the ARO algorithm to add stochastic dynamic behavior to the creation process of the initial binary combinations of features. Second, it utilizes the Adaptive β-hill climbing (ABHC) method in the evolution process of ARO to improve its global search and exploration abilities. Third, it uses the Mixed Opposition-based Learning (MOBL) approach in the evolution process of ARO to explore the opposite solutions of the best and worst rabbits in the population of rabbits. Finally, it employs binary conversion methods to compute binary subsets of features from the real numbers produced by the evolution processes of the ARO and ABHC algorithms. The performance of BIARO, six machine learning classifiers, and nine efficient, popular, nature-inspired FS algorithms was investigated using 21 real-life HDDs from different fields. According to experimental results, BIARO achieved excep­ tional results in real-life HDDs, with average accuracy values between 0.69 and 1, average precision values in the range of 0.67 to 1, average F1 scores in the range of 0.67 to 1, average Recall values in the range of 0.67 to 1, and a perfor­ mance improvement rate between − 2 and 66. Furthermore, statistical verification methods were employed to evaluate the dependability of the experimental results. The statistical results show that BIARO scored the highest rank based on the fitness values for 14 HDDs, with a p-value of 0.001. Besides, it shows that it scored the highest rank based on the number of selected features for 18 HDDs, with a p-value of 0.001. All experimental and statistical results provide evidence that BIARO is an efficient FS method for HDDs.
